Neonates of the Siamese crocodile emerge from their eggs at a total length of approximately 28.5 cm [Lb = approximately 28.5 cm], a value derived from comparative data on the congeneric Mugger crocodile Crocodylus palustris, which shares a similar reproductive ecology. Hatchlings at this stage are lecithotrophic larvae that rely entirely on their yolk reserves during the first days of life before the onset of exogenous feeding. Under controlled incubation conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 31 °C [T = 31 °C], the embryonic development period lasts 74 days [ab = 74 days], a duration that falls well within the 68 to 80 day range typically reported for the species. The wet body mass recorded immediately following eclosion averages 90.8 grams [Wwb = 90.8 grams], although some studies, such as that by PlatNomy in 2012, report a somewhat higher figure of 121.6 grams, suggesting that hatchling mass may vary with maternal investment or incubation humidity. This relatively modest initial mass underlines the heavy reliance on the yolk-sac larva stage for early nutrition.

Sexual maturation in Crocodylus siamensis follows a protracted trajectory that is strongly influenced by thermal conditions. For individuals maintained at a constant temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the time since birth at which females reach puberty is approximately 6 years (approximately 6 years since birth) [tp = approximately 6 years since birth], with males maturing at a comparable age of about 6 years [tp = about 6 years] as well. These estimates, based on data from the related C. palustris, align well with field observations that place female maturation between 8 and 10 years and male maturation between 12 and 15 years under variable natural conditions. The attainment of reproductive maturity is marked by gonadal activation and the development of secondary sexual characteristics. At the onset of puberty, individuals are estimated to have a total length of 200 cm [Lp = 200 cm], a size threshold again inferred from C. palustris. Males, which ultimately grow larger than females, typically reach this pubertal milestone at a greater body length of 260 cm [Lp = 260 cm].

Adult body size in Siamese crocodiles exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with males attaining substantially larger dimensions than females. The ultimate total length for adult females reaches 320 cm [Li = 320 cm], while males can achieve a maximum documented length of 400 cm [Li = 400 cm], reflecting the competitive advantages of larger body size in male-male interactions during the breeding season. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of reproductively active females averages approximately 150,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 150,000 grams], whereas adult males attain a far greater asymptotic mass of about 350,000 grams [Wwi = about 350,000 grams]. This disparity in body mass, a factor of more than two, is among the more extreme examples of sexual size dimorphism observed within the Crocodylidae family. Such considerable somatic investment in growth by males likely delays the onset of their own reproductive efforts, as resources are channeled into achieving competitive body size rather than early breeding.

Under stable laboratory conditions maintained at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan of Crocodylus siamensis reaches 49 years [am = 49 years]. This extended longevity is typical of large crocodylians, which exhibit slow life-history strategies characterized by delayed maturity and low adult mortality rates. The species' reproductive output under these conditions is comparatively modest. Females typically lay between 15 and 50 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 15 and 50 eggs per clutch], and under the same thermal regime, they produce approximately one clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately one clutch per year]. Because multiple clutches are not laid within a single annual cycle, the overall maximum reproductive rate is constrained by this single seasonal event. The combination of relatively small clutch sizes and a single annual reproductive bout reflects an energy-conserving strategy suited to the species' tropical freshwater habitats.

Nesting females construct mound nests composed of vegetation and soil along riverbanks and seasonally flooded wetlands, where the heat of decomposition supplements the incubating temperature of 31 °C [T = 31 °C] required for optimal embryonic development. The age at which individuals reach functional sexual maturity, approximately 6 years since birth [tp = approximately 6 years since birth] for both sexes at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], is relatively early compared to some larger crocodylids such as the saltwater crocodile, which often delays maturation until a decade or more. This earlier pubertal timing may be an adaptation to the more seasonal and less stable freshwater environments of Southeast Asia, where early reproduction can offset higher juvenile mortality. The total length at puberty of 200 cm [Lp = 200 cm] for females and 260 cm [Lp = 260 cm] for males represents a significant fraction of their respective ultimate sizes, indicating that substantial somatic growth continues even after reproductive activity begins. Conservation efforts must account for this extended maturation period when estimating population recovery times after harvest or habitat loss.
